summary: Explains that URI structure is defined by its scheme and owner, and cautions against independent standards that mandate particular URI paths or structures on sites they do not own. It is best-practice guidance.

plainLanguage.summary: When a specification says a URL must look a certain way, it is usually fixing a shape that the owner of that web site has not agreed to. This document explains the five ways that goes wrong, and what a specification may and may not say about the parts of a URI: the scheme, the host part, the path, the query and the fragment.

questions: can a specification mandate a url path
why should a specification not define a uri path prefix
subtitle: Best practices for specifications that want to fix the shape of a URI, and why most of them should not.

tldr.problem: URIs often carry structured data, and specifications keep trying to standardize that structure, for example by fixing a path prefix or naming a query parameter. When someone other than the owner of the URI does that, the result collides, goes stale, or breaks deployment.
tldr.mechanism: The document gives per-component rules: a specification MUST NOT fix a path prefix, MUST NOT constrain the authority or the query format, and MUST NOT define structure inside the fragment identifier, unless it updates the URI scheme registration itself.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 7320, updates RFC 3986, and turns much of the earlier document's requirements into guidance. It also points to alternatives: link relations, URI templates and registered well-known paths.

facts.label: Path prefix rule
facts.value: Specifications MUST NOT define a fixed prefix, unless allowed by the scheme definition

facts.label: Exception to the path rule
facts.value: Registered well-known URIs, as specified in RFC 8615

facts.label: Scheme substructure
facts.value: MUST be done by modifying BCP 35, an exceptional circumstance

facts.label: Authority rule
facts.value: Only the scheme registration may define its structure or semantics

facts.label: Document status
facts.value: Best Current Practice, which updates RFC 3986

today: RFC 8820 is a Best Current Practice published in June 2020. It obsoletes RFC 7320 and updates RFC 3986, and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why Fixing the Shape of a URI Goes Wrong
sections.content:
URIs very often include structured application data. This might include artifacts from filesystems, often occurring in the path component, and user information, often in the query component. In some cases there can even be application-specific data in the authority component, for example when an application is spread across several hostnames to enable a form of partitioning or dispatch.

Implementations can impose further constraints on the structure of URIs. Many web servers use the filename extension of the last path segment to determine the media type of the response, and prepackaged applications often have highly structured URIs that can only be changed in limited ways, often just the hostname and port on which they are deployed.

Because the owner of the URI is choosing to use the server or the application, this can be seen as reasonable delegation of authority. However, when such conventions are mandated by a party other than the owner, it can have several potentially detrimental effects:

  • Collisions. As more ad hoc conventions for URI structure become standardized, it becomes more likely that there will be collisions between them, especially since servers, applications and individual deployments have their own conventions.
  • Dilution. When the information added to a URI is ephemeral, this dilutes its utility by reducing its stability, and can cause several alternate forms of the URI to exist.
  • Rigidity. Fixed URI syntax often interferes with desired deployment patterns. If an authority wishes to offer several applications on a single hostname, it becomes difficult or impossible to do if their URIs do not allow the required flexibility.
  • Operational difficulty. Supporting some URI conventions can be difficult in some implementations. Specifying that a particular query parameter be used with http URIs can preclude web servers that serve the response from a filesystem, and an application that fixes a base path such as /v1 makes it impossible to deploy other applications with the same prefix on the same host.
  • Client assumptions. When conventions are standardized, some clients will inevitably assume that the standards are in use when those conventions are seen, which can lead to interoperability problems. If a specification documents that the sig URI query parameter indicates that its payload is a cryptographic signature for the URI, it can lead to undesirable behaviour.

Publishing a standard that constrains an existing URI structure in ways that are not explicitly allowed by RFC 3986, usually by updating the URI scheme definition, is therefore sometimes problematic, both for these reasons and because the structure of a URI needs to be firmly under the control of its owner.
sections.plainLanguage: Five things go wrong when someone fixes a URI shape they do not own. Two specifications can end up using the same pattern. The pattern can become stale, so the same resource has several addresses. It can make it impossible to run two applications on one host. It can be hard for servers to support. And clients that recognise the pattern may act on it in ways nobody intended.

sections.title: Who This Document Is For
sections.content:
The document's guidelines and requirements target the authors of specifications that constrain the syntax or structure of URIs or parts of them. Two classes of such specifications are called out specifically.

  • Protocol extensions: specifications that offer new capabilities that could apply to any identifier or to a large subset of possible identifiers, for example a new signature mechanism for http URIs, metadata for any URI, or a new format.
  • Applications using URIs: specifications that use URIs to meet specific needs, for example an HTTP interface to particular information on a host.

Requirements that target the generic class of specifications apply to all of them.

The document says it ought not to be interpreted as preventing the allocation of control of URIs by parties that legitimately own them or have delegated that ownership. For example, a specification might legitimately define the semantics of a URI on IANA's web site as part of the establishment of a registry.

There may be existing IETF specifications that already deviate from the guidance in this document. In those cases it is up to the relevant communities, those of the URI scheme and any relevant community that produced the specification in question, to determine an appropriate outcome, for example updating the scheme definition or changing the specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules are for people writing specifications that tell others how to build URIs. They do not stop a site owner from deciding the shape of its own addresses, and they do not require every existing specification to be rewritten.

sections.title: Schemes and Authorities
sections.content:
This section of the document updates RFC 3986 by advising specifications how they should define structure and semantics within URIs. The best practices differ depending on the URI component in question.

Schemes. Applications and extensions can require the use of one or more specific URI schemes; it is perfectly acceptable to require that an application support http and https URIs. However, applications ought not preclude the use of other URI schemes in the future, unless they are clearly only usable with the nominated schemes. A specification that defines substructure for URI schemes overall, for example a prefix or suffix for scheme names, MUST do so by modifying BCP 35, which is an exceptional circumstance.

Authorities. Scheme definitions define the presence, format and semantics of an authority component in URIs. All other specifications MUST NOT constrain or define the structure or the semantics for URI authorities, unless they update the scheme registration itself or the structures it relies upon, for example the DNS name syntax. For example, an extension or application cannot say that the foo prefix in https://foo_app.example.com is meaningful or triggers special handling in URIs, unless they update either the http URI scheme or the DNS hostname syntax. Applications can nominate or constrain the port they use when applicable, for example an application called BarApp could run over a port that is properly registered.
sections.plainLanguage: The scheme says which protocol is being used and the authority says which host and port. Only the specification that defines the scheme may say what goes in the authority, so an application cannot claim that a particular host name prefix means something special unless the scheme or the DNS rules are changed.

sections.title: Paths
sections.content:
Scheme definitions define the presence, format and semantics of a path component in URIs, although these are often delegated to the applications in a given deployment.

To avoid collisions, rigidity and erroneous client assumptions, specifications MUST NOT define a fixed prefix for their URI paths, for example /myapp, unless allowed by the scheme definition. One such exception to this requirement is registered well-known URIs, as specified by RFC 8615.

This does not apply to applications defining a structure of a URI's path under a resource controlled by the server, because the prefix is under the control of the party deploying the application, so collisions and rigidity are avoided and the risk of erroneous client assumptions is reduced. For example, an application might define app_root as a deployment-controlled URI prefix, and application-defined resources might then be assumed to be present at {app_root}/foo and {app_root}/bar.

Extensions MUST NOT define a structure within individual URI components, for example a prefix or suffix, again to avoid collisions and erroneous client assumptions.
sections.plainLanguage: A specification cannot claim that every URL of a certain shape belongs to it. A server operator, on the other hand, is free to decide that its own resources live under a path of its choosing, because it owns that part of the name space.

sections.title: Queries
sections.content:
The presence, format and semantics of the query component of URIs are dependent upon many factors and can be constrained by a scheme definition. Often they are determined by the implementation of the resource itself.

Applications can specify the syntax of queries for the resources under their control. However, doing so can cause operational difficulties for deployments that do not support a particular form of a query, for example a site that wishes to support an application using static files that do not support query parameters.

Extensions MUST NOT constrain the format or semantics of queries, to avoid collisions and erroneous client assumptions. For example, an extension that indicates that all query parameters named sig indicate a cryptographic signature would collide with potentially preexisting query parameters on sites, and would lead clients to assume that any matching query parameter is a signature.

The document also notes that HTML constrains the syntax of query strings used in form submission, and that new form languages are encouraged to allow the creation of a broader variety of URIs, for example by allowing the form to create new path components.
sections.plainLanguage: An application can decide how its own query strings look. A general extension cannot, because the parameter name may already mean something else on someone else's site.

sections.title: Fragment Identifiers
sections.content:
Section 3.5 of RFC 3986 specifies fragment identifiers' syntax and semantics as being dependent upon the media type of a potentially retrieved resource. As a result, other specifications MUST NOT define structure within the fragment identifier, unless they are explicitly defining one for reuse by media types in their definitions, for example as JSON Pointer does.

An application that defines common fragment identifiers across media types not controlled by it would engender interoperability problems with handlers for those media types, because the new, non-standard syntax is not expected by those handlers.
sections.plainLanguage: The part of a URI after the hash sign is read by whatever handles the content, so only the format that describes the content may say what goes there. An application that invented its own fragment syntax would break every handler that did not know about it.

sections.title: Alternatives to Fixing URI Structure
sections.content:
Given the issues described in the introduction, the most successful strategy for applications and extensions that wish to use URIs is to use them in the fashion for which they were designed: as links that are exchanged as part of the protocol, rather than statically specified syntax. Several existing specifications can aid in this.

  • RFC 8288 specifies relation types for web links. By providing a framework for linking on the web, where every link has a relation type, context and target, it allows applications to define a link's semantics and connectivity.
  • RFC 6570 provides a standard syntax for URI Templates, which can be used to dynamically insert application-specific variables into a URI, enabling such applications while avoiding impinging upon URI owners' control of them.
  • RFC 8615 allows specific paths to be reserved for standard use on URI schemes that opt into that mechanism, http and https by default. The document notes, however, that this is not a general escape valve for applications that need structured URIs.

Specifying more elaborate structures in an attempt to avoid collisions is not an acceptable solution and does not address the issues described in the introduction. Prefixing query parameters with myapp_, for example, does not help, because the prefix itself is subject to the risk of collision, since it is not reserved.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a better way than fixing shapes: say what a link means rather than what it looks like, and build the parts of the address that vary from a template. Reserving a well-known path is possible too, but only for a few schemes and only through the process that document describes.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document says it does not introduce new protocol artifacts with security considerations. It prohibits some practices that might lead to vulnerabilities. For example, if a security-sensitive mechanism is introduced by assuming that a URI path component or query string has a particular meaning, false positives might be encountered, due to sites that already use the chosen string. The reader is referred to RFC 6943 on issues in identifier comparison for security purposes.

The IANA considerations section states that the document has no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing here is a new protocol, so there is nothing new to attack. The risk avoided is the one where a mechanism assumes that a particular path or query string means something, and then meets a site that was already using that string for something else.

viz.caption: THE FIVE EFFECTS OF FIXING A URI SOMEONE ELSE OWNS

items.title: Collisions
items.text: Two specifications end up using the same pattern, and the servers and applications disagree.

items.title: Dilution
items.text: The information is ephemeral, so the URI loses its stability and several forms of it exist.

items.title: Rigidity
items.text: The fixed syntax makes it impossible to run several applications on one host.

items.title: Operational difficulty
items.text: Servers that serve from a filesystem or share a prefix cannot support it.

items.title: Client assumptions
items.text: Clients that recognise the pattern act on it, sometimes wrongly.

viz.caption: THE PARTS OF A URI THIS DOCUMENT COVERS
WHO MAY DEFINE THE STRUCTURE OF EACH PART

cells: A specification that adds substructure to scheme names MUST modify BCP 35.
Other specifications MUST NOT constrain it, unless they update the scheme or the DNS name syntax.
The scheme, often delegated to the application
Specifications MUST NOT define a fixed prefix, except registered well-known URIs.
Extensions MUST NOT constrain the format or semantics of queries.
The media type of the resource
Other specifications MUST NOT define structure within it.

viz.caption: THE ALTERNATIVES THE DOCUMENT POINTS TO

items.title: Web Linking
items.text: Relation types give every link a type, a context and a target, so meaning travels with the link.

items.title: URI Templates
items.text: A standard syntax fills the variable parts of a URI at runtime, leaving the owner in control.

items.title: Well-known URIs
items.text: Specific paths can be reserved for standard use, but only on schemes that opt in.
